content: 1. The 2008 paper by Manary provides a comprehensive guide on the management of acute malnutrition, focusing on evidence-based practices for healthcare professionals. 2. Minetti's 2009 study compares the NCHS and WHO 2006 growth standards for weight-for-height (W/H) but does not evaluate the performance of mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC). 3. Ojo's 2000 research estimates the prevalence of malnutrition at the population level using MUAC z-scores and weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ). However, it does not compare anthropometric indicators or include nutritional interventions. 4. O’Neill's 2012 study examines the predictive power of MUAC-for-age in determining mortality risk but does not address nutritional rehabilitation. 5. The 1999 WHO manual provides detailed guidance for physicians and senior health workers on managing severe malnutrition, emphasizing clinical protocols and interventions. 6. A 2009 joint statement by WHO and UNICEF outlines the use of WHO child growth standards for identifying severe acute malnutrition in infants and children. 7. Another joint statement from 2007 by WHO, WFP, the UN Standing Committee on Nutrition, and UNICEF discusses community-based management of severe acute malnutrition. 8. Myatt, Khara, and Collins (2006) review methods for detecting severely malnourished children in community settings to facilitate their admission into therapeutic care programs. 9. Berkley et al. (2005) compare weight-for-height and MUAC in assessing severe malnutrition among hospitalized children in rural Kenya. 10. Fernandez et al. (2010) evaluate the accuracy of MUAC in detecting severe wasting using the new WHO growth standards. 11. Bekele et al. (2009) report on a community-based therapeutic feeding program that exclusively uses MUAC as an admission criterion. 12. Myatt and Duffield (2007) review survey data from 1992 to 2006 to compare weight-for-height and MUAC in estimating the prevalence of acute undernutrition. 13. Pinoges (2002) compares MUAC (<125 mm) and weight-for-height indicators (W/H <80% of the median and W/H <-2 z-score) using data from Médecins Sans Frontières, Action Contre la Faim, and UNHCR databases. 14. Ciliberto et al. (2005) conduct a controlled trial comparing home-based therapy with ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) to standard therapy for treating malnourished Malawian children. 15. Ciliberto et al. (2006) explore the use of RUTF in home-based therapy for children with edematous malnutrition. 16. Nielsen et al. (2004) examine the impact of supplementary feeding on malnourished children during the war emergency in Guinea-Bissau (1998–1999). 17. Defourny et al. (2009) provide evidence for large-scale distribution of milk-based fortified spreads as a novel approach to addressing acute malnutrition in high-burden regions. 18. Amthor, Cole, and Manary (2009) evaluate the use of RUTF in home-based therapy for malnutrition during a food crisis in rural areas. 19. Linneman et al. (2007) conduct a large-scale operational study on home-based therapy with RUTF for childhood malnutrition in Malawi. 20. Manary et al. (2004) investigate the effectiveness of home-based therapy using RUTF for severe malnutrition. 21. Oakley et al. (2010) compare the efficacy of RUTF containing 10% milk versus 25% milk in treating severely malnourished children. 22. Sullivan et al. (1991) assess the long-term effects of in-patient rehabilitation on persistent diarrhea and malnutrition. 23. Roberfroid et al. (2010) discuss the utility of MUAC in screening for severe acute malnutrition and propose future directions. 24. Mei et al. (1997) develop a MUAC-for-height reference and compare it to other nutritional status screening indicators. 25. Ulijaszek and Kerr (1999) analyze measurement errors in anthropometry and their implications for assessing nutritional status. 26. Ayele et al. (2012) evaluate the reliability of measurements taken by community-trained anthropometrists in rural Ethiopia. 27. Mwangome et al. (2012) assess the reliability and accuracy of anthropometric measurements performed by community health workers among infants under six months in rural Kenya. 28. Akinbami et al. (2010) identify body mass composition as a predictor of admission outcomes among hospitalized Nigerian children under five. 29. Beckett et al. (2000) examine the effects of energy and micronutrient supplementation on anthropometry in undernourished children in Indonesia. 30. Bejon et al. (2008) estimate the fraction of hospital admissions and deaths attributable to malnutrition among children in rural Kenya. 31. Blankhart et al. (1977) report on low arm circumference and its role in nutritional rehabilitation of children under five. 32. Briand et al. (1986) evaluate the usefulness of nutritional indices and classifications in predicting mortality among malnourished children. 33. Cheek et al. (1977) investigate the significance of cell mass relative to body length in protein-calorie malnutrition. 34. Chevalier et al. (1996) study immuno-nutritional recovery in children with severe malnutrition. 35. Collins et al. (2006) provide an overview of the management of severe acute malnutrition in children. 36. Connor and Manary (2010) monitor the adequacy of catch-up growth among moderately malnourished children receiving home-based therapy using MUAC in Southern Malawi. 37. Doherty et al. (1998) explore the relationship between zinc supplementation and rehabilitation from severe protein-energy malnutrition, noting increased mortality with higher-dose regimens. 38. Dramaix et al. (1993) examine the relationship between serum albumin concentration, arm circumference, edema, and subsequent mortality risk in children in Central Africa. 39. Erinoso et al. (1993) identify prognostic factors, including anthropometric and biochemical parameters, in severely malnourished hospitalized Nigerian children. 40. Hossain et al. (2009) share experiences in managing severe malnutrition in a government tertiary treatment facility in Bangladesh. 41. Isanaka et al. (2011) estimate the duration of untreated acute malnutrition in children from Niger. 42. Kumar et al. (1996) validate the use of MUAC for screening undernutrition in children. 43. Lagrone et al. (2010) demonstrate the effectiveness of locally produced ready-to-use supplementary food in treating moderate acute malnutrition in operational settings. 44. Lapidus et al. (2009) evaluate the prognostic accuracy of WHO growth standards in predicting mortality in a large-scale nutritional program in Niger. 45. Lapidus et al. (2009) assess mortality risk among children admitted to a large-scale nutritional program in Niger. 46. Loewenstein and Phillips (1973) evaluate arm circumference measurement for determining nutritional status during an acute malnutrition epidemic in Nigeria following the civil war. 47. McDowell and King (1982) interpret arm circumference as an indicator of nutritional status. 48. Manary and Sandige (2008) discuss the management of acute moderate and severe childhood malnutrition. 49. Minetti et al. (2009) analyze the impact of transitioning from NCHS growth references to WHO 2006 growth standards in a therapeutic feeding program in Niger. 50. Ojo et al. (2000) explore the use of anthropometric and clinical parameters for early identification and categorization of nutritional risk in preschool children in Benin City, Nigeria. 51. O’Neill et al. (2012) investigate child mortality as predicted by nutritional status and recent weight velocity in children under two in rural Africa. 52. Savadogo et al. (2007) describe the management of severe acute malnutrition in an urban nutritional rehabilitation center in Burkina Faso.
